name: Control types & categories
why: Almost every exam asks you to classify a control. Learn the six types (preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive) and four categories (managerial, technical, operational, physical) and you answer these in seconds.

name: Zero Trust planes
why: The PDP/PEP split is pure memorization that CompTIA tests directly. Control plane decides, data plane enforces.

name: Change management
why: An entire objective (1.3) rides on a short list of artifacts. The backout plan is the single most-asked item in the domain.

name: Crypto decision points
why: You rarely need the math — you need to pick the right primitive. Hash for integrity, encrypt for confidentiality, sign with the private key, salt plus stretch for passwords.

name: PKI & certificates
why: Certificate questions repeat with small variations: CSR carries the public key, CRL is a list, OCSP is a query, wildcards cover one label deep.

name: Social engineering families
why: The highest-frequency identification questions on the exam. The delivery channel names the attack — email, SMS, voice, look-alike domain, compromised third-party site.

name: Threat actors & motivations
why: Match resources plus sophistication plus motive and the actor falls out. Nation-state equals funding and stealth; organized crime equals money; hacktivist equals publicity; insider equals existing access.

name: Malware identification
why: Classify by how it spreads and what it does. Self-propagating equals worm, disguised equals trojan, condition-triggered equals logic bomb, hidden from the OS equals rootkit.

name: Application attacks
why: Recognize the payload signature and name the fix. Parameterized queries, output encoding, path canonicalization, bounds checking, anti-CSRF tokens.

name: Network attacks & indicators
why: Objective 2.4's indicator list is finite and gets asked verbatim. Learn what each indicator implies and which attack produces it.

name: Password attacks
why: Spraying versus brute force versus rainbow tables is a guaranteed distinction question, and the mitigation is always MFA plus rate limiting.

name: Core mitigations
why: Objective 2.5 is a short list that answers dozens of scenario questions. Lateral movement equals segmentation; too many admins equals least privilege; unknown binaries equals allow list.

name: Zones, segmentation & appliances
why: The densest scoring area in Domain 3. Know which box does what, where it sits, and that IDS detects while IPS blocks inline.

name: Secure access & protocols
why: Protocol swap questions are free points: Telnet to SSH, FTP to SFTP, LDAP to LDAPS. Add the 802.1X trio and ESP versus AH.

name: Cloud responsibility & models
why: Shared responsibility appears in every cloud scenario. IaaS means you own the guest OS; SaaS means you still own identity and data.

name: Data states & classification
why: Three states, one control set each: at rest equals disk or file encryption, in transit equals TLS or IPsec, in use equals enclaves. Classification then drives every handling answer.

name: Backup & recovery objectives
why: RPO versus RTO and full versus differential versus incremental are near-certain questions, and hot/warm/cold sites map straight to cost and speed.

name: Incident response process
why: The seven phases in order, and the ability to tell containment from eradication from recovery, answers a large block of Domain 4 by itself.

name: Forensics handling
why: Order of volatility and chain of custody are memorization with guaranteed payoff. Memory before disk, document every handoff, hash before and after.

name: Log sources & correlation
why: Objective 4.9 is entirely 'which data source answers this question'. Flow for who talked to whom, endpoint for what ran, packet capture only when you need content.

name: Identity, access & MFA
why: The single largest scoring cluster on the exam. Access control models, the MFA factor categories, SAML versus OAuth versus OIDC, and just-in-time privileged access.

name: Vulnerability management
why: CVE names it, CVSS scores it, context prioritizes it, a rescan proves it. False positive versus false negative shows up almost every time.

name: Detection tooling
why: Tool-to-job matching is fast, reliable scoring. SIEM correlates, EDR responds on the host, DLP stops data leaving, NAC gates the port, SPF/DKIM/DMARC secure mail.

name: Hardening & baselines
why: The hardening checklist repeats across every platform: remove software, disable ports, change defaults, add EDR and a host firewall, enforce the baseline.

name: Document hierarchy
why: Policy, standard, procedure, guideline — distinguished by their verbs. 'Must' is mandatory, 'should' is advisory, numbered steps are a procedure.

name: Risk math
why: AV times EF equals SLE; SLE times ARO equals ALE. These are the only calculations on the exam and they are free points once drilled.

name: Risk process & register
why: Four strategies (mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept), a register with named owners, and the BIA metrics RTO, RPO, MTTR, MTBF.

name: Agreements & third-party risk
why: The acronym set is pure recall: SLA, MOU, MOA, MSA, SOW, NDA, BPA. Add right-to-audit and SOC 2 Type II and the objective is covered.

name: Compliance & assessments
why: Due diligence discovers, due care acts. Known versus unknown environment testing, and passive versus active reconnaissance, are reliable single-fact questions.

name: Awareness essentials
why: Objective 5.6 rewards one instinct: report through the sanctioned channel, never interact, and verify out of band.
